newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares rise in kerb after monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: India shares rise in kerb after monetary policy.

text.p: A new six-month monetary policy announced by India's central bank on Saturday pepped up sagging market morale and pushed share prices up in kerb trade, brokers and analysts said.
State Bank of India (SBI.BO share was quoted at 225 rupees ($6.3) against 218.75 previous close. Reliance rose to 197/198 from 196.75 and TISCO to 175/176 from 172.50.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) eased liquidity conditions by cutting cash reserve ratio (CRR) requirements for banks to 10 percent from 12 percent and allowed banks to buy stocks in the secondary market.
The market had been expecting a CRR cut of 1.0-1.5 percentage points.

"The CRR cut will definitely inject liquidity into the market but more importantly for stock markets, allowing banks to invest in secondary market will psychologically give a good boost," said Hemendra Kothari, chairman at DSP Financial Consultants, the Indian affiliate of Merrill Lynch.
Kothari said though the amount of money injected by banks in bonds, mutual funds and shares will not be very large, the move itself would cheer sentiment.

"It shows RBI is becoming more responsive to market requirements and is willing to tackle the recent slowdown in industrial activity and exports," said Devesh Kumar, strategist at securities firm W.I. Carr.
He said the decision to allow banks to invest in listed shares would cheer sentiment.
"Earlier, there was a shyness in allowing any public institution to trade in the secondary market. This is a departure from RBI's earlier attitude," Kumar said.
"Five percent of incremental deposits would amount to around 30 billion rupees which is not a very big amount but it will give respectability to secondary market operations," he said.
"It shows secondary market investments are being treated as genuine and not speculative," he added.
